chapter_theme: The king has the wedding city perfumed and strewn, calls his princes and the elephant Arasuva, has it dressed in gold and gems, and rides out with the kings in a procession of drums, flags, dust and musth that draws the women's eyes, while Maruci tells the Vidyadhara king, whose host rises to meet him.

cast.role: the king of Podanam, host of the wedding, taken as the speaker of the orders and the rider of the elephant
the royal princes told to ride out with the king
the attendants who run to call the elephant
the keeper who calms and equips the elephant Arasuva
the man who dresses the elephant for the wedding ride, unnamed; perhaps the keeper
the women who hold fly-whisks for the rider
the allied kings who rise with the king
the bangled women of the route
the handsome young men of the procession
the dancing women with a peacock gait
the messenger who carries word to the Vidyadhara king
the Vidyadhara king's host, rising to receive the king

923.reading: The king orders that the inner city be turned to scented mire with saffron and sandal paste, wrapped in aloe smoke under a cloud-like canopy and strewn with gold powder, and that the wedding be got up.
923.nuance: The poet counts splendour by waste: paste is poured until the city is mud. The speaker is not named; he is taken to be the king because 924 names the commander of the drum-sounding army who gives the next orders.
923.event: The king orders the city perfumed and strewn with gold powder for the wedding.

924.reading: Having sent the officer off with these orders, the king tells the young princes to put on garlands and gold necklaces, mount rutting elephants and ride with him.
924.event: The king commands the princes to adorn themselves and ride out with him on elephants.

925.reading: The king calls for a particular tusker to be brought, its white tusks like a moon cut in two and set in place, its small red-spotted eyes and fierce rut able to master even the vyala.
925.nuance: The speaker is carried over from 924 and is not named here.
925.event: The king calls for the chosen elephant to be brought.

926.reading: At a word that shows the king's mind, attendants run calling the elephant Arasuva, and its keeper climbs the neck of the maddened young tusker, steadies it with a fearsome voice and takes up his work from above.
926.nuance: அரசுவா is taken here as the elephant's name; the sense of the word is not fixed and the verse is read loosely.
926.event: The keeper mounts the maddened elephant and calms it with his voice while attendants call for it.

927.reading: The keeper who has played with Arasuva and knows its ways loosens its girth, ties on a new rope, fastens a second, leads it out of the stall and tells the men of the earth to mount.
927.nuance: The keeper gives the elephant to the riders with the words 'let those of the earth mount'; the tamer's craft is spent before the king's ride begins.
927.event: The keeper refits the elephant's ropes, brings it from the stall and invites the riders to mount.

928.reading: Another rides up and takes the great cloth rope, the golden chains are loosened and the rear girths tied, and the man who will dress the beast to the king's wish bids the forked-goad bearers gather round.
928.nuance: Who mounts and who is called 'the later one' is not named; the dresser may be the keeper of 926 or another.
928.event: The dresser readies the elephant's rope and girths and calls the goad bearers around it.

929.reading: The garlanded man has the grass of cane and paddy ears that tangled between the tusks cleared, the dust and fallen blossoms swept off and red water sprinkled.
929.nuance: The garlanded one is taken to be the dresser, since the next verses continue his work; he could also be the king.
929.event: The tusks are cleared of fodder and the ground sprinkled with red water.

930.reading: With saffron paste, sandal and conch-pattern work the dresser marks the diamond-bright tusks and adorns the beast's sides and all that lies near them.
930.event: The dresser paints the tusks and adorns the elephant's sides.

931.reading: The elephant is fitted with a gold-clasp, a gem-studded forehead-band, an embossed head-cover over its face, a blazing gold plate on the brow and a fly-whisk garland at the root of its ear.
931.event: The dresser fits the elephant's head with gold, gems and a whisk garland.

932.reading: Garlands are hung and a cushion spread; two ropes are tied slantwise like rainbow bands over cloud, gem-strings hang, gold powder is scattered and flags are set up that flash like lightning in cloud.
932.event: The dresser finishes the elephant with cushion, ropes, gems, powder and flags.

933.reading: When the elephant is dressed, the one who guards the earth to the ocean's rim mounts to the praise of kings, his gem necklaces gleaming, earrings flashing like rainbows and women holding fly-whisks, and he shines like a burning sun.
933.nuance: The rider is taken to be the king, since 934 gives the king's white umbrella; a bridegroom is not excluded by the Tamil.
933.event: The king mounts the dressed elephant amid praise and fly-whisks.

934.reading: Under one raised silver umbrella with pearl strings over his crown, the king, who tends all the world evenly so that it cools together, drives his great musth elephant on and passes through the rich city to its wonder.
934.nuance: The cooling umbrella is a sign of the king's protection, but here it is displayed as a part of the ride, not tested as a duty.
934.event: The king rides his elephant through the city under the white umbrella.

claims.claim: a king guards the whole world evenly so that all of it is cooled

935.reading: As the king rises with the other kings, the drumbeat blends with the mulavu drum, and at every gate in every direction the sound swells like the sea breaking on its shore.
935.nuance: The sound is the main figure here, set against the sea; the metre is short and the grammar clipped.
935.event: The king and the kings rise to the sound of drums that fill every gate.

936.reading: Pipes, drums, small drums and other instruments with their kin, bangles and horns rise together like thunder-clouds so that those who hear lose their senses.
936.nuance: Several instrument names and the last word are rare and the sense is held loosely.

937.reading: Flower-rain falls, smoke whirls up, bees scatter, the directions grow dark, gem-lamps blaze, flags rise and the streets and quarters show in variegated stripes.
937.nuance: The last line turns on rare words and is read loosely.

938.reading: Flags and umbrellas crowd in and darken the air, crowns and gleaming earrings flash like a rising sun, and as the king's army rises with its anklets night and day seem to mingle.
938.nuance: Dark umbrellas and bright crowns together make the procession both night and day.

939.reading: The horses' hooves raise dust and the musth of the elephants pours down in rain and turns to mud, so that people, stunned, can scarcely see the streets.
939.nuance: The pairing of dust and musth-mud is the verse's whole point; the last line is read loosely.

940.reading: The flapping ears of the war elephants, the neighing of the horses and the anklets of the armed warriors blend so that no other sound can be heard.
940.nuance: Three noises are named and then none are heard: the poet shows a crowded street by deafness.

941.reading: Women of the bangles, their composure broken by the beauty of the young men, call from both sides of the way, laughing and ripening into desire, and even the mature feel it.
941.nuance: நிறை (composure) is undone here by sight alone; the last line widens the effect to the ripe and wise, but its grammar is hard and the sense is held loosely.
941.event: Women along the route lose their composure at the young men and call out, laughing, with desire.

942.reading: With the sound of musicians and the thunder of the drums, the peacock-like gait and gestures of the dancing women and the crowds of kings' kin, the rich city has no room left.
942.event: Musicians and dancers fill the city with the kings' kin.

943.reading: Maruci goes and tells the Vidyadhara king of rare fame that the lord of Suramai is coming, and the telling of the strong army that rises to receive him is hard to give.
943.nuance: The addressee and the 'tall one of the gem crown' are read as the Vidyadhara king; the verse has no direct naming of him.
943.event: Maruci announces the coming of the lord of Suramai and the Vidyadhara army rises to receive him.

944.reading: The elephants of the mountain lord's host are like black hills, its long banners like mountain streams and its young warriors like tigers of the high hills, an army set rising.
944.nuance: The host is taken to be the Vidyadhara's from 943; the verse says only 'the army of the lord of the great mountain'.

945.reading: Their army on earth comes so that the ground sinks and their army on the mountain so that the mountain is crushed, while the sea's waves draw aside, and with tall hill-like elephants in rows steady footing is hard to find.
945.nuance: The last line has a broken syntax and the sense is read loosely.

946.reading: The poet says that if horses are said to enter the clouds they have the manner of clouds, and that the aloe-smoke that enters among them is the praise of those who send it up.
946.nuance: The play on cloud, horse and smoke is read loosely; the sense of the last line rests on rare grammar.

links.note: Verse 902 orders gate-arches, gold pots and a decorated city; verse 923 carries the order on to saffron and sandal mud, aloe smoke and gold powder.
links.teaches: The wedding is prepared in stages, from the frame of the city to its scent, and the second order goes beyond what the first asked.

links.note: In 917 the king seats Maruci on a gold-fronted elephant before him; in 933 the king himself mounts the dressed elephant.
links.teaches: The elephant first honours the guest's envoy and only afterwards carries the king, so the ride is a courtesy given in order of rank.

links.note: Verse 927 shows a keeper who knows the elephant's ways re-roping it and handing it to its riders; Tirumanthiram 2023 sets five rutting elephants in the body that will not come to the post of the Agamas' teaching.
links.teaches: The same craft of the keeper is both a working skill here and the picture of a discipline that fails without a teaching there.

gains.a: The verse shows a keeper's craft but not why such taming might matter beyond the ride.
gains.b: The verse names the inner elephants but has no scene of a keeper who actually succeeds with one.

links.note: Verse 934 shows the king's white umbrella raised in the ride that cools the world; Kural 389 says the world lives under the umbrella of a king who can bear bitter words.
links.teaches: The umbrella cools only for a king who has the character the Kural names, which the display of the ride cannot show.

gains.a: The verse lacks the condition of character that makes the umbrella a shelter.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any picture of the umbrella in its pomp as the world sees it.

links.note: Verse 934 shows a king riding an elephant under a high umbrella; Naladiyar 21 says kings who rode elephants under umbrellas like the moon over a hill have been carried off.
links.teaches: The same pomp that the Soolamani shows as the king's splendour is the thing the Naladiyar sets against death, so the display is also a reminder of its end.

gains.a: The verse lacks any hint that the splendour of the ride is brief.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks the scene whose brightness gives its warning weight.

links.note: Verse 936 gives the roar of pipes, drums and horns at the wedding ride; Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sound for a wedding may sound the same day for the bridegroom's funeral.
links.teaches: The wedding's noise is the same instrument as the funeral's, so the Naladiyar turns the verse's joy into a warning without changing the sounds.

gains.a: The verse lacks any thought that its music could change meaning.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks the wedding's full noise that makes its reversal strong.

links.note: Verse 941 shows women along the route losing their composure at the sight of the young men; Kural 1254 says the restraint she boasted of passes beyond concealment into the open.
links.teaches: The public street is the occasion where the Kural's private breaking of restraint becomes visible to all.

gains.a: The verse lacks the woman's own account of the restraint she once claimed.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the crowded occasion that draws desire out in public.

links.note: In 901 Maruci goes to the lord of Suramai to announce the Vidyadhara's arrival; in 943 he goes the other way to tell the Vidyadhara king that the lord of Suramai is coming.
links.teaches: The messenger crosses between the two courts in both directions, so each side is first hosted and then hosting, and the welcome is mutual.

links.note: Verse 944 gives the host's standing by its look: elephants like hills, banners like streams, warriors like tigers; Kural 768 says an army without striking power still gains standing from its martial bearing.
links.teaches: A host at a wedding is shown by its bearing alone, which is the standing the Kural says an army can have even before it fights.

gains.a: The verse lacks any statement of what such bearing is worth.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of the bearing it names.

source_issues: Verse 924 line 2 and 933 line 1: pulli after a vowel sign repaired in the edition.
Verse 928: stanza printed in 8 half-lines and joined into 4 lines.
Verses 923 to 925: the speaker is not named and is taken to be the king from 924.
Verse 926: the word அரசுவா is read as an elephant's name; this is not fixed.
Verses 935 to 946: short metre with clipped grammar and rare words; many readings are held loosely.
